1) in a threshold public good game with a large population, a small number of players with a low cost of provision will be the most likely contributors to the public good, and will be the only contributors in the long run; and 2) the addition of an extra player with low cost of provision may spoil the barrel by destabilizing a successful team.

(1) the correlation between players’ costs of provision and valuations for the public good determines the likelihood of collective action; (2) the addition of one extra player can destabilize a successful team; and (3) the likelihood of successful collective action is higher when the pool of possible team members is limited to those whose valuations for the goods are high enough to cover the costs of providing it.
